newsitem.title: FRANCE: France wants Iraqi oil deal to come into force.
newsitem.headline: France wants Iraqi oil deal to come into force.

text.p: France called on Wednesday for new negotiations to ensure that a U.N. resolution allowing Iraq to use the proceeds of oil sales for food and medical supplies comes into force as soon as possible.

"Our aims are first to ensure peace in the region and to ensure that the Iraqi leaders are no longer in a position to harm their neighbours or their own people," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure told Europe-1 radio.

"After long negotiations, Iraqi leaders and the international community had agreed on the oil for food resolution...We call for dialogue to ensure that the accord is brought into force as fast as possible," Lamassoure said.
The U.S. State Department said on Tuesday that the U.N. plan to let Iraq sell some oil to raise hard currency for food and medical supplies was off "for some time".

United Nations Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Sunday postponed implementation of the oil-for-food plan, expected later this month. He said he could not send U.N. staff to monitor it because he feared for their safety.

Under the plan, Iraq was to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other supplies for its citizens. The United States and other countries had sought assurances that proceeds from the oil sales would be used to meet humanitarian needs, and not to build up Iraq's military.

Asked whether Paris condemned the Iraqi offensive, and invited to respond to accusations of betrayal from Jalal Talabani, leader of the Kurdish faction under attack from Baghdad, Lamassoure said: "France had no commitments towards this individual.
"France's reaction has been similar to that of the greater part of the international community...After a period of tension we should go back to peace and dialogue."

France, one of the 1991 Gulf War allies, withheld support for a first U.S. missile attack on Iraq on Tuesday, saying Baghdad had not breached U.N. resolutions by sending its troops into Kurdish areas of northern Iraq.

Lamassoure made no direct comment on a second U.S. missile strike on Iraqi air defence positions in southern Iraq on Wednesday to neutralise possible resistance to President Bill Clinton's decision on Tuesday to extend the southern Iraq air-exclusion zone.
"France has warned Iraq and our foreign minister has written to his counterpart to demand the withdrawal of (Iraqi) troops. From the start we have called for moderation and dialogue," he said.

France is one of the allies enforcing no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq but as Iraq's biggest creditor and erstwhile arms supplier, it is keen to ease the U.N. economic embargo against Baghdad.
